decisions.reason: Although it had its own launch page, an address-autocomplete service is relatively generic and peripheral to the firm's announced energy-platform direction, so the sunk cost and public commitment are limited enough that management would likely discontinue it if traction was modest.

A grid-fee database fits the firm's data-centric regulated-energy business closely enough that prior database investment and the public standalone offering would make management inclined to continue it, despite its niche Austrian scope.

This service is close to the firm's core analytical and compliance-oriented offer, so accumulated development effort and strategic fit with modular SaaS make escalation of commitment likely to keep it on the market.

An end-customer tariff database with several models suggests comparatively higher investment and visible commitment, and it aligns well with the firm's platform and data strategy, making management unlikely to withdraw it.

Custom web services build on existing capabilities but are less productized and can be folded back into consulting or project work, so management has less need to defend them as a distinct market offering if results disappoint.

A postal-code lookup service is a generic utility with weak strategic centrality to regulated energy processes, so despite a standalone page the firm would have relatively little escalation pressure to keep it as a separate product.
